extracted.intended_audience: poets and writers preparing submissions for literary journals and magazines
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for researching appropriate literary journals and preparing/submitting poems, short stories, and creative nonfiction to literary magazines and journals, including cover letters, simultaneous submissions, formats, fees, and follow-up practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your market
rubrics_metrics.description: Before beginning the submission process, it is essential to research the market to determine which publications are the best venues for your writing. Your publishing success rests on one axiom: Know your market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use databases (Poets & Writers Literary Magazines database), read sample issues and archives, compare your work to pieces they publish, consult contributors' notes and acknowledgements in books to see where authors publish. Purchasing recent issues or browsing bookstore/library periodical sections helps develop a feel for editorial voice, tone, viewpoint, and mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the publication before submitting
rubrics_metrics.description: It's important to read the literary magazines in which you'd like to publish before you submit your work, so that you can determine whether they are a good match for you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peruse online archives and current/archived content; read contributors' notes and bios; compare your background and interests to those of published writers; mention specific pieces you admire in the magazine (briefly) to show familiarity when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow each publication's submission guidelines exactly
rubrics_metrics.description: When you submit your work, always be certain to follow the guidelines of each publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidelines may specify acceptable genres or themes, submission months, word/page limits, limits on number of poems per submission, whether to include a cover letter, and accepted submission methods (website, e-mail, Submittable, or mailed SASE). Many journals refuse to read work not submitted in accordance with their guidelines, so find guidelines on the publication website or in print and stick to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect genre/theme and length restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some magazines specify genres or themes in which they are or are not interested and may set word limits, page limits, or limits on number of poems per submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm that your piece fits the magazine’s stated genres/themes and length constraints before submitting; tailor submissions to outlets that publish work similar to yours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not submit previously published work unless allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: Most literary magazines do not consider previously published work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm each publication's policy on previously published pieces; withdraw or disclose prior publication when required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate submission channels and include required materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Most accept submissions through their website, via e-mail, or through platforms like Submittable; some mailed submissions may require a self-addressed stamped envelope (SASE).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the requested format (file types, subject lines, cover letter requirements) and include SASE when mailing if requested so the editors can respond or return material as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether to pay reading fees and understand fee options
rubrics_metrics.description: Some magazines charge a reading fee (typically a couple dollars) or offer paid options promising faster response periods; many charge nothing or offer free reading periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine for yourself whether you are comfortable paying fees; watch for announced free reading periods and factor fees into submission budgeting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous submissions: follow individual publication policy and notify upon acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: The literary world is divided about submitting the same piece to multiple publications at once; some discourage or explicitly forbid simultaneous submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow each publication’s stated stance. If they allow simultaneous submissions, most require notification if the piece is accepted elsewhere. If they forbid it, do not submit simultaneously. If the publication doesn’t specify, you may indicate in your cover letter that you are submitting simultaneously. If one publication accepts your piece, immediately contact other publications to withdraw the submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover letters should be short and factual; avoid summarizing or arguing for the piece
rubrics_metrics.description: It is customary—and sometimes required—to include a short cover letter with each submission. Avoid using the letter as a platform to discuss the merits or themes of the work or to summarize your writing as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep cover letters simple and straightforward: include a brief bio listing prior publications (if applicable), optionally mention work published by the magazine that you admire to show familiarity, and address the specific editor when possible. Do not use the cover letter to justify or analyze your submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notify and withdraw promptly if accepted elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: If you send your submission simultaneously to more than one publication, and one of them accepts it, immediately contact the other publications to let them know that you’re withdrawing your submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely withdrawal respects editors' time and resources and prevents duplicate publication conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep organized records of submissions and costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Track how many times you’ve submitted a poem, story, or essay; the amount of money spent on fees; the status of submissions; and elapsed time since submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tools such as the Poets & Writers Submission Tracker or other trackers (spreadsheets, Duotrope, Chill Subs) to manage submissions, deadlines, and responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research contributor bios and acknowledgements to target suitable markets
rubrics_metrics.description: Read contributors’ notes and bios to compare your background and interests to those of the writers whose work is included in those particular magazines. Look to book acknowledgements for the names of journals that publish authors you admire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this information to find journals that publish work similar to yours and to craft targeted submissions that align with the publication’s editorial community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support the publishing community where feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: Purchasing recent issues of several publications helps you decide where to submit and supports the publishing community as a good literary citizen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if you don't publish in all the journals you buy, buying back issues or subscribing can be a way to learn and give back.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use available directories and resources to find markets and opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplement Poets & Writers’ databases with other resources such as Open Reading Periods, Grants & Awards database, CLMP Directory, Heavy Feather Review’s Where to Submit, Chill Subs, Duotrope, and NewPages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult these directories to find journals currently open for submissions, contests, presses, and other opportunities; consider workshops (e.g., Mapping the Maze) to plan submissions strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: When in doubt, disclose simultaneous submissions in the cover letter
rubrics_metrics.description: If a publication does not specify its stance on simultaneous submissions, you could indicate in your cover letter that you’re submitting the same piece to other magazines at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This transparency reduces potential friction and demonstrates professional courtesy to editors who may prefer to be informed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect modest payment or contributor copies, not large sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Many literary magazines and journals will offer you a modest payment for the writing they accept, sometimes by giving you a free copy, or contributor’s copy, of the issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set realistic financial expectations for magazine publication; some journals pay small honoraria, others only contributor copies.
